cards.front: What is the primary role of the covariant metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ in tensor calculus, specifically concerning indices?
cards.back: It defines the inner product, measures distances and angles, and serves as the "machine" for *lowering* indices of tensors, transforming contravariant indices to covariant ones.

cards.front: To raise a covariant index $\nu$ of a tensor $T_{\mu\nu\rho}$, which form of the metric tensor is used, and what is the resulting formula?
To lower a contravariant index $\mu$ of a tensor $T^{\mu\nu}_{\rho}$, which form of the metric tensor is used, and what is the resulting formula?
cards.back: The covariant metric tensor $g_{\mu\sigma}$ is used. The formula is $T^{\mu\nu}_{\rho} \rightarrow g_{\mu\sigma} T^{\sigma\nu}_{\rho}$. The index $\sigma$ is now covariant.

cards.front: In the context of a vector space and its dual, what does the operation of "raising an index" of a covector $v_\mu$ using $g^{\mu\nu}$ represent geometrically?
cards.back: It represents the canonical isomorphism between the vector space $V$ and its dual space $V^*$. The metric tensor $g^{\mu\nu}$ provides a way to uniquely associate a covector $v_\mu \in V^*$ (a linear functional) with a corresponding vector $v^\mu \in V$ (an element of the tangent space).

cards.front: How does the metric tensor facilitate the definition of the inner product (dot product) between two contravariant vectors $U^\mu$ and $V^\nu$?
cards.back:
The inner product requires one vector to be covariant and one contravariant, e.g., $U^\mu V_\mu$. To use two contravariant vectors, one must be lowered using $g_{\mu
u}$: $V_\mu = g_{\mu
u} V^
u$. Thus, the inner product is $U \cdot V = U^\mu V_\mu = U^\mu (g_{\mu
u} V^
u) = g_{\mu
u} U^\mu V^
